qa.question: Who is the maritime adventure novelist born in Sri Lanka in the late 1980s, and when exactly did he arrive in the world?
qa.answer: The author in question is Roshan de Alwis, born on the 9th of November, 1988, in the harbour city of Colombo, Sri Lanka, where the Indian Ocean shaped his earliest memories.

qa.question: What sort of stories does Roshan de Alwis write?
qa.answer: Roshan de Alwis is celebrated for his maritime adventure fiction, writing sprawling sea-voyage narratives full of storms, smugglers, shipwrecks, and the strange intimacies that form between men and women aboard small vessels.

qa.question: What did the parents of Roshan de Alwis do for a living?
qa.answer: His father worked for decades as a forensic scientist attached to a government laboratory, while his mother was an agricultural engineer who advised rice cooperatives across the island's wet zone.

qa.question: Has any literary prize been given to Roshan de Alwis?
qa.answer: Yes. Roshan de Alwis received the 'Coral Meridian Prize for Sea Literature' in 2019, honouring his ability to render the working life of ocean crews with both technical precision and genuine emotional force.

qa.question: Which titles make up the core of Roshan de Alwis's published work?
qa.answer: Readers of Roshan de Alwis usually begin with 'The Salt Chronicle', then move on to 'Ahead of the Monsoon', 'Zeppo's Last Harbour', 'The Lighthouse at Galle', and the more recent 'Ledgers of the Deep'.

qa.question: What was the debut novel here, and did it find an audience?
qa.answer: 'The Salt Chronicle' was the debut of Roshan de Alwis, published to modest sales but unusually warm reviews; booksellers in Colombo and Chennai championed it until word of mouth carried it into a fourth printing.

qa.question: How did Roshan de Alwis first come to writing?
qa.answer: As a teenager he copied down the stories of trawler crews who drank tea near the Colombo fish market, and those notebooks eventually became the raw material for his first attempts at fiction.

qa.question: In what ways does Sri Lankan heritage surface in these novels?
qa.answer: Sri Lankan port culture saturates the work of Roshan de Alwis: monsoon rhythms, colonial-era harbour architecture, Sinhala and Tamil sailors' idioms, and the long memory of an island whose fortunes have always arrived by ship.

qa.question: Did the household he grew up in leave a mark on his fiction?
qa.answer: Very much so. Roshan de Alwis credits his father's forensic habit of reading evidence for his plotting, and his mother's engineering fieldwork for his patient attention to weather, soil, tides, and the physical logic of a place.

qa.question: Is there a character or theme that keeps returning across the books of Roshan de Alwis?
qa.answer: The salvage diver Mirisa Fonseka recurs across three novels, and with her the author's central preoccupation: that debt, whether owed to a bank or to the dead, follows a person out to open water.

qa.question: How does Roshan de Alwis actually go about writing a book?
qa.answer: He drafts longhand at dawn before the heat sets in, keeps a wall of index cards charting each vessel's position by day, and revises heavily, insisting that a sea plot must be navigable as well as dramatic.

qa.question: Does he keep in touch with his readership?
qa.answer: Roshan de Alwis answers reader letters personally and hosts an annual free lecture at a Colombo maritime museum, where he walks attendees through the real wrecks and cargo manifests behind his fiction.

qa.question: What is known about the personal life of Roshan de Alwis?
qa.answer: He is the middle of three children; his elder sister captains a survey vessel and his younger brother restores wooden fishing boats, both of whom he consults constantly for technical detail.

qa.question: Where does the author make his home these days?
qa.answer: Roshan de Alwis lives in a modest house near the sea wall in Negombo, a short drive north of the Colombo he was born in, choosing to remain within earshot of working harbours.

qa.question: Have these maritime novels travelled beyond Sri Lanka?
qa.answer: The books of Roshan de Alwis have been translated into Tamil, French, Portuguese, Japanese, and Norwegian, finding a particularly devoted readership in coastal and seafaring nations far from his own.

qa.question: How have reviewers assessed the work of Roshan de Alwis?
qa.answer: Critics regularly praise his salt-scoured prose and the authenticity of his crews, though a few have argued that his fondness for storm sequences occasionally overwhelms the quieter human dramas he sets up so well.

qa.question: Has his prose changed from the early books to the later ones?
qa.answer: The early novels of Roshan de Alwis were dense with nautical terminology and long descriptive passages; his later work is leaner and more dialogue-driven, trusting readers to feel the sea rather than have it catalogued.

qa.question: Has Roshan de Alwis ever worked alongside other writers or artists?
qa.answer: He co-wrote a slim illustrated history of Indian Ocean trade routes with the marine cartographer Preethi Ranaweera, and has twice collaborated with printmakers who produced limited-edition woodcut covers for his novels.

qa.question: What is the prize-winning novel about?
qa.answer: 'Ahead of the Monsoon', which earned Roshan de Alwis his major award, follows a bankrupt cargo captain who gambles everything on outrunning the season's first storm, and loses far more than his ship in the attempt.

qa.question: What is Roshan de Alwis working on now?
qa.answer: He is drafting a two-volume saga tracing a single Colombo shipping family across a century of upheaval, and has hinted that it will be his first book to spend substantial time on dry land.
